title: Fats & Oils
subtitle: 1850–1900 · Light Goes to Oil Wells, Butter Goes to the Factory: Kerosene, Margarine, Cottonseed, Lever’s Soap and the Palm Kernel

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Civil War and the whalers

entries.label: The Civil War cripples American whaling
entries.loc: Charleston, the Pacific and Bering Strait
entries.hint: Like the Revolution and the War of 1812, the Civil War crippled American whaling. Owners idled ships, reflagged them or sank them: in 1861 whaleships loaded with stones were sunk in Charleston harbor as the ‘Stone Fleet’. The South’s whale-oil trade was cut off completely, demand in the North fell as kerosene became the illuminant of choice, and Confederate raiders, above all the Alabama and the Shenandoah, destroyed whalers: the Shenandoah burned the Hector, Edward Carey, Pearl and Harvest at Ponape in 1865.
entries.note: ANCHOR (two books read): Dolin, Leviathan (2007; 2016 ed.) pp.340–347 (PDF pp.340, 347); Bockstoce, Whales, Ice, and Men (1986) pp.110–125 (PDF pp.110, 115, 129; the Shenandoah and the ‘Civil War in Bering Strait’). The 1865 date of the Ponape burnings follows the context of the Shenandoah’s Arctic cruise in Bockstoce.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The margarine laws of Missouri, the United States and Germany

entries.label: Missouri outlaws margarine; states ban yellow margarine
entries.hint: In 1881 Missouri outlawed the manufacture, sale or possession with intent to sell of margarine, while other states forbade colouring it yellow to look like butter or even required it to be dyed pink. Van Stuyvenberg says some states simply banned it, and that an attempt to have such laws declared unconstitutional failed; Mueller adds that congressional hearings on margarine began in the early 1880s and continued through 1950.
entries.note: SECONDARY (two books read): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011) pp.253–254 (Missouri 1881; the farm lobby; hearings to 1950) and van Stuyvenberg (ed.), Margarine: An Economic, Social and Scientific History 1869–1969 (1969) ch.7, pp.283–285 (state laws, the unconstitutionality challenge). Not all state laws were read.

entries.label: The US federal oleomargarine law taxes the new fat
entries.hint: After violent controversy, a federal law of 1886 allowed margarine to be sold only as ‘oleomargarine’, imposed licences of $600 for manufacturers, $480 for wholesalers and $48 for retailers, and a manufacturing tax of 2 cents a pound, with packaging and bookkeeping rules. It had no rules on colouring, though colour was the main reason the state laws had failed; its purpose, van Stuyvenberg says, was the protection of dairy farming at the expense of the margarine industry.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): van Stuyvenberg (1969) ch.7 ‘The federal law of 1886’, pp.285–286. The author’s reading of the act’s purpose and Bannard’s analysis of the motives of its advocates are given there.

entries.label: Germany passes its first Margarine Act
entries.hint: Germany’s first Margarine Act (1887) followed a violent anti-margarine campaign of about 1886 when butter prices were low: margarine shops had to be marked, blending butter into margarine was forbidden, tubs had to bear the word ‘margarine’, and the fat had to be sold as a cube. The Frankfurter Margarine Gesellschaft had begun making margarine in 1872, and German protection from 1879 sheltered the young industry. Inadequate enforcement left the act with almost no effect.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): van Stuyvenberg (1969) ch.7 ‘Germany’, pp.290–291, citing Schüttauf, Die Margarine in Deutschland und der Welt (1966).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Ivory and Mark Twain’s two beaters

entries.label: Meiji Japan eats meat: the emperor’s meal of 1872
entries.hint: The Meiji government set out to build industry and a conscript army, and the learned men of the time, who had gathered their information from the West, believed that the Japanese had poorer physiques than Westerners because they did not eat meat or dairy products. The public was urged to eat meat and drink milk, especially after the news spread in 1872 that the emperor had eaten meat, and for the next few years such a diet was regarded as the mark of a civilised person. Meat went into soldiers’ meals, and Western-style restaurants opened in the cities, where meat and beer proved the most appealing items. Ishige calls this the resumption of meat eating; the first Japanese prohibition on it had been Emperor Temmu’s decree of 675.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Ishige, The History and Culture of Japanese Food (2001), PDF p.153 (1872 and the campaign), with p.160 for the imperial navy serving beef from 1869, and pp.64–66 for Temmu’s decree. The book is about meat and dairy foods generally; fat enters through the cooking of the next entry. Compare fats-600-1000::o2.

entries.label: Western restaurants and the cutlet: Japan meets frying fat
entries.hint: In the early Meiji years Western-style restaurants, sometimes in hotels, were extraordinarily expensive and served only a tiny upper class, with menus built on meats, fats and oils. In the late 1880s Japanese cooks trained in them opened yoshokuya for the urban public, and by the turn of the century Tokyo had fifteen to sixteen hundred. An English recipe book of 1872 had introduced the cutlet as veal or lamb, floured, egged, crumbed and fried in a little butter; by about 1900 the breaded cutlet was standard fare in these restaurants but Japanized: pork or beef, lard or beef fat in place of butter, and enough fat to immerse the meat, with some restaurants deep-frying it in a pot of sesame oil as for tempura. Western-style cooking at home was still uncommon and used vegetable oil. Ishige notes that a nation accustomed to cooking without oil or fat took Western and Chinese cooking to be ‘so oily, so heavy’; pork-cutlet restaurants appeared from the 1920s and the dish became tonkatsu.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Ishige, The History and Culture of Japanese Food (2001), PDF pp.84 (the first impression), 166 (the restaurants, with Ito 1990 for the count) and 257–258 (the cutlet). Compare fats-1500-1750::e3 for tempura, the Edo-period frying that came first.

entries.label: Ivory: a name from the Psalms and a floating white soap
entries.hint: Procter & Gamble trademarked Ivory on 18 July 1879, a name Harley Procter found in Psalm 45 (‘out of the ivory palaces’), with a chequerboard wrapper designed for the grocer’s shelf. The story that Ivory floated by accident, from an air-whipped batch, cannot be traced to credible testimony; the company had experimented with floating soaps for at least a dozen years. Ivory taught the firm ‘not just how to sell, but how to learn’.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Dyer, Dalzell & Olegario, Rising Tide: Lessons from 165 Years of Brand Building at Procter & Gamble (2004) ch.1 (PDF pp.37–40). The first accidents of the floating soap are told there as legend.

entries.label: Mark Twain overhears the two beaters: fake butter, bogus olive oil
entries.hint: In Life on the Mississippi (1883) Mark Twain overhears two ‘beaters’ gloating about the fortunes to be made on cheap, easy-to-make butter and olive-oil substitutes — for Twain, bogus oil and fake butter symbolised the artificiality of American life. By then fifteen margarine plants were operating in the United States, with about $7 million in sales.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; Twain not read): Mueller (2011) pp.251–253, who also cites the New England Journal of Medicine of 1863 calling the olive oil sold in America ‘very seldom pure’; the plant and sales figures are Mueller’s and are not sourced in the passage.

entries.label: Mège-Mouriès: butterfat comes from beef suet
entries.hint: The chemist Hippolyte Mège-Mouriès, working at Napoleon III’s own farm at Vincennes on a commission to find a cheaper butter substitute that kept better, observed that fasting cows still give milk and concluded that butterfat must come from the cow’s body fat. Pressing beef suet at 30–40°C he got a fat melting at 20–25°C — in the language of the day, oleo-margarine — which he churned with milk into ‘beurre économique’. The patent was lodged on 15 July 1869 and granted on 2 October.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): van Stuyvenberg (1969) ch.1 pp.6–7 (Napoleon III’s interest, Vincennes, the suet process; the patent F.P. 86480 ‘lodged 15 July 1869, granted 2 October’; the plate caption gives the grant as 15 July, an inconsistency in the book). Chevreul’s ‘margarine’ of 1813 was an impure palmitic acid: the product’s name is a historical accident.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Margarine, cottonseed, the packers, Arctic whaling, palm kernels, groundnuts and Lever

entries.label: The groundnut coasts of Senegambia
entries.hint: A groundnut trade grew from the Gambia from 1834 and in Senegal under French firms, whose rivalry between Bordeaux and Marseille shaped policy, and for whom profitability declined from 1881. West African groundnut farms, like the cocoa farms of the Gold Coast and the palm exports of the coastal forests, grew from indigenous initiative; groundnut exports from northern Nigeria took off only after the railway reached Kano in 1911.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly book read, which mainly gives notes here): Hopkins, An Economic History of West Africa (2020 ed.) Introduction (PDF pp.41, 43, 47), citing Swindell & Jeng, Migrants, Credit and Climate: The Gambian Groundnut Trade, 1834–1934 (2006) and Klein 1972. A fuller chapter-level account was not read.

entries.label: The packers turn the pig into lard, candles, soap, stearin and oleomargarine
entries.hint: Pork and lard were Cincinnati’s trade in the 1840s, when packers turned body parts once wasted into lard, glue, candles and soaps and could pay more for each hog; Chicago’s packers of the 1850s boiled the rest into tallow and lard for candles and soap. In the chemical laboratories the packers installed in the 1880s and 1890s lard and tallow were joined by oleomargarine and stearin, and a butcher complained of competing with a packinghouse ‘lard’ made of cottonseed oil and stearine.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Cronon, Nature’s Metropolis (1991), the pork-packing and by-products sections (PDF pp.245, 265–268). The packers’ own laboratories and the butcher’s complaint are Cronon’s citations of contemporary sources.

entries.label: Coconut oil: textile-mill lubricant, soap fat and the fish-and-chip shop
entries.hint: Coconut oil’s first industrial use in Europe was as a lubricant in textile mills, and it then became important to soap makers; schooners and tramp steamers went to the Pacific islands for copra, which was easier to ship than fresh nuts. Because it was available all year from colonial possessions, whereas the soap-boilers’ animal fat was seasonal, it undercut them; large-scale advertising of branded soaps then put the small local soap-boilers out of business, and, Harries argues, the men with copper pans and no soap to sell turned to frying fish and chips, a trade dating from the mid-1800s.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter; a thesis rather than a record): Kiple (2000) II.E.2 pp.389–390 (PDF pp.426–427), after Harries 1988. The fish-and-chip link is Harries’s interpretation; the chapter quotes a ‘Nut Lard’ advertisement of 1912 (see fats-1900-1960).

entries.label: Bowhead and baleen: Arctic whaling, and the 1871 disaster
entries.hint: In 1848 Captain Thomas Roys took the bark Superior through Bering Strait, the first whaleship to do so. The price of whalebone had doubled between 1840 and 1844, and substitute illuminants were already pushing down the price of sperm oil, so the combined value of the right whale’s oil and whalebone overtook the sperm whale’s. In 1871 the ships were trapped in ice off Point Belcher and abandoned; the insurance payments were invested in textile mills and other ventures nearer home as merchants withdrew from the declining whaling grounds.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Bockstoce, Whales, Ice, and Men (1986) ch.1 (PDF pp.25, 33) and the chapter on the disaster of 1871 (PDF pp.156, 164). The number of ships lost in 1871 is not given in the passages read. The American fleet shrank to 321 in 1870 (Dolin, Leviathan, PDF p.393).

entries.label: India takes up the groundnut: 1,000 hectares in 1850, seventy times that by 1895
entries.hint: Achaya traces the groundnut’s four types, Virginia, Peruvian Runner, Valencia and Spanish, which were all cultivated first in south India and later in western India between 1850 and 1900; he thinks the large Brazilian type, which came by way of Africa, and the small Peruvian type, from Manila or China, probably entered India independently. The area under groundnut was just 1,000 hectares in 1850 and seventy times that by 1895. Kiple adds the market behind it: Europe could not meet its demand for olive oil, so a peanut-oil trade grew up, with the nuts coming mainly from West Africa and then from India after the opening of the Suez Canal. Achaya notes that production rose from 250,000 tonnes in 1910 to 1.5 million in 1930, and that groundnut is now by far India’s largest oilseed crop, with about a tenth eaten as nuts or in cooking and the rest crushed for oil.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Achaya, Indian Food: A Historical Companion (1994), PDF p.258 (scanned and OCR’d, so the figures should be rechecked against the printed page); Kiple & Ornelas, eds., The Cambridge World History of Food (2000), PDF p.402 (Peanut chapter) for the Suez Canal and the European market. Neither passage names the buyers or the ports. Compare ec6 for the West African side and fats-1500-1750::x2 for the peanut in China.

entries.label: The palm-kernel trade: margarine and Lever’s soap
entries.hint: From the middle of the century palm oil was joined by palm kernels: British imports of ‘nuts and kernels’ from West Africa rose from 592 tons in 1855 to 34,186 tons by 1895, driven, Lynn says, by the mass market for cheap margarine, in which palm kernel oil was used extensively. Old Calabar’s kernel exports rose from 1,000 tons in 1869 to 10,000 tons in 1887, following William Lever’s ‘self-washing’ soap made from kernel and coconut oil for working-class consumers in hard-water areas; the flat prices of the 1890s checked but did not kill the trade.
entries.note: ANCHOR (two scholarly books read): Lynn (1997) Introduction p.3 (PDF p.23; the tonnages, with her note 19) and Law (1995) (PDF p.191; kernels from Old Calabar; Lever’s soap).

entries.label: Cottonseed: from garbage to table oil
entries.loc: The American South and New Orleans
entries.hint: Popular Science Monthly noted in 1894 that cottonseed had been garbage in 1860, fertiliser in 1870, cattle feed in 1880 and ‘table food and many things else’ in 1890. In 1879 alone 73,782 barrels of cottonseed oil left New Orleans for Europe, over half bound for Italy, where it was used to adulterate olive oil, and much of the rest went into oleomargarine; an Atlanta paper joked that Italians had increased output by setting a cask of cottonseed oil at the foot of every tree.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history): Mueller (2011) pp.251–252 (the Popular Science Monthly remark; the 1879 shipments; the British consul at Livorno). The shipment figures are Mueller’s and were not checked against the port records.

entries.label: European oil-palm plantations in Africa fail
entries.hint: From the late nineteenth century Europeans created experimental oil-palm plantations in West and west-central Africa; one of the earliest was founded in Gabon in 1870 by Catholic missionaries, but like most such ventures it was unsuccessful. European planters were highly specialised and exposed to trade swings, many lacked capital, and they spent money planting where natural groves already held more palms than local farmers could harvest.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter): Kiple (2000) II.E.3 p.398 (PDF p.435), citing Hopkins 1973 and Martin 1988; the Gabon mission from a personal communication by E. J. Mulder (1968).

entries.label: Jurgens buys the margarine patent; the Dutch butter houses go into margarine
entries.hint: In 1871 the Dutch butter house Jurgens in Oss, a family firm 100 years in the butter trade, learned of the French patent and bought Mège’s knowledge for 60,000 francs (there was then no patent law in the Netherlands); his British, American and Prussian patents went to other buyers in 1873–74. High prices were making butter exports to England difficult, and Jurgens’s international butter connections carried the new fat abroad. Margarine went on sale in Paris in 1872; the Frankfurter Margarine Gesellschaft started in Germany that year. Another Dutch butter firm, Van den Bergh, followed.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): van Stuyvenberg (1969) ch.1 pp.7–12 and ch.7 p.290; Mueller (2011), the passage on Mège-Mouriès, puts the sale of the patent to Jurgens and Van den Bergh in 1871 and gives European margarine output as 300,000 tons by 1895, with hydrogenated and fractionated oils about 90 per cent of European fats by 1923.

entries.label: Lever Brothers: Sunlight Soap from 1884, Warrington, Port Sunlight
entries.hint: William Lever set up a wholesale grocery, Lever & Co., in 1877; in 1884 it registered the trademark ‘Sunlight Soap’, and Lever made his soap at a leased factory at Warrington from 1885 to 1889, Lever Brothers Ltd being registered as a private company in May 1890 and as a public company with £1.5 million capital in 1894. Lever’s concern for secure supplies of vegetable oil, and his belief in crushing palm kernels where they grew, shaped the later Unilever supply chains.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Fieldhouse, Unilever Overseas (1978) ch.1 (PDF p.19; Lever & Co. 1877; Sunlight trademark 1884; Warrington 1885–1889; Lever Brothers Ltd registered May 1890 and a public company in 1894) and ch.6 (PDF p.176; Lever’s preoccupation with vegetable-oil supplies and the crushing of kernels where they grew). Port Sunlight is not in the passages read.

entries.label: Lever’s Sydney office buys Pacific copra and Australian tallow, then crushes copra at Balmain, 1888–1900
entries.hint: In December 1888 Lever Brothers opened an office in Sydney with a double job: to repack and distribute the imported products of Port Sunlight across the Australian colonies, and to buy copra from the Pacific Islands and Australian tallow and send them home as raw materials. William Lever visited Australia in 1892, noting that South Australia’s tariff on imported soap was 4d a pound against 1d if the brand name were stamped in the colony, and again in 1895, when he reorganised the agents and bought a waterfront site at Balmain, where a copra-crushing mill and oil tanks were built at once. The soap works followed in 1899 and began operating in October 1900, owned by Lever Brothers Ltd (Australia), incorporated in New South Wales on 31 December 1899.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Fieldhouse, Unilever Overseas: The Anatomy of a Multinational, 1895–1965 (1978), PDF p.38 (book pp.64–65), who adds that evidence for the 1890s is very limited and the decision to manufacture soap in Australia cannot be dated precisely. The Pacific side of the copra, who grew and cut it, is not in the passage. Compare fats-1900-1960::ec13.

entries.label: Syria’s sesame oil, about 1892: soaked, hammered, floated, broiled and ground
entries.hint: Law’s Grocer’s Manual, published about 1892, says sesame is widely cultivated in Syria and describes how the oil is made there. The grain is soaked in water for 24 hours and put into an oblong pot lined with cement, where two men work a wooden hammer of 20 lb, with no attempt to mash the kernels. The skins are separated in a tub of water salted enough to float an egg, so that the bran sinks and the kernels stay on the surface. The seeds are then broiled in an oven and sent to the mill; from the millstone the oil drops into a jar, thick, dark yellow and sweet.
entries.note: SECONDARY (book read, quoting a quotation): Bedigian’s ‘Sesame’ chapter in Kiple & Ornelas, eds., The Cambridge World History of Food (2000), PDF p.450, quoting Law’s Grocer’s Manual (c.1892) as cited in David (1970) p.54. The year is the manual’s date, not an observation date, and the manual names no town or maker. Compare fats-300bc-600ad::th3 for sesame in India and fats-8000bc-1200bc::th1 for the Akkadian ‘oil-plant’.

entries.label: Kerosene and Drake’s well end whale-oil lighting
entries.hint: Abraham Gesner, a Canadian geologist, refined kerosene in the late 1840s from bituminous tar; it burned cleaner and brighter than any other illuminant and gave its light at a far lower cost per unit. By the end of the 1850s there were thirty-three kerosene plants in the United States, and in 1859 ‘Colonel’ Edwin Drake drilled a well seventy feet deep at Titusville and struck oil, the ‘most devastating blow’ to the whale oil industry. Lard oil and other substitutes were already eating into sperm oil on grounds of cost.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Dolin, Leviathan (2007; 2016 ed.) pp.365–369 (PDF pp.365, 368–369), citing Beaton 1955 on Gesner and Tower’s History of the American Whale Fishery. For the landscape of the first oil boom see Petrolia (Brian Black, 2000).

entries.label: Oleo-margarine: suet, milk and a churn
entries.hint: Margarine was made by pressing beef suet into oleo-margarine and churning it with milk; it had to be sold under names that did not suggest butter — Mège’s ‘beurre économique’ became ‘Margarine Mouries’ because butter-like names were illegal. In 1872 it was put on sale in Paris as margarine, but was sold abroad as ‘margarine butter’.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): van Stuyvenberg (1969) ch.1 p.7 (the process, the 1872 sale, the naming).

entries.label: Bertolli follows the emigrants: Italian oil in the Americas
entries.hint: By the 1890s the Italian banker Francesco Bertolli was making more money from olive oil than finance, selling to the Mediterranean immigrants of New York, Philadelphia and Chicago and then across the United States and Latin America; his son Giulio opened Brazil, on muleback through Minas Gerais, selling brooms and giving a tin of oil free with each, until he sold only oil.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history): Mueller (2011) p.251 (the Bertolli story; his source is not named in the passage).

entries.label: Whaleships on the Japan Grounds help open Japan: Cooper at Edo, the Lagoda, Perry, 1845–1854
entries.loc: Uraga Bay, Edo, Nagasaki and the Japan Grounds
entries.hint: When American whalemen began to hunt the Japan grounds they came into contact with the Japanese, and those contacts, Dolin writes, helped lay the foundation for Commodore Perry’s expedition. In 1845 Captain Mercator Cooper of the Sag Harbor whaleship Manhattan took shipwrecked Japanese sailors to Uraga Bay, off Edo; the emperor had the ship supplied free of charge, ringed it with guards and boats, and told Cooper never to return. In June 1848 fifteen crewmen deserted the New Bedford whaleship Lagoda for the Japanese shore and were held for ten months, some in open cages, until the USS Preble took them home in April 1849. Perry reached Edo in July 1853, drew on information from whalemen including Cooper, and signed the Treaty of Kanagawa on 31 March 1854, which opened ports for provisioning, coal included, and for shipwrecked sailors. Dolin judges that Melville overstated the whalers’ part; the US government also wanted coal for its steamships.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Dolin, Leviathan: The History of Whaling in America (2007), PDF pp.275–278. The Japanese side of the encounter is told only through American accounts. Ellis, Men and Whales (1991), PDF p.111, adds that the Bonin Islands, found by Captain Coffin of Nantucket in 1824, were a centre of Yankee whaling. Compare fats-1750-1850::ec12.

entries.label: Germany turns protectionist: the margarine boom behind a tariff
entries.hint: Germany’s change to a protectionist policy in 1879 shielded the new margarine industry from foreign competition; the Frankfurter Margarine Gesellschaft had started in 1872 and the German industry faced, van Stuyvenberg says, ‘an almost insatiable demand’, especially from the working population of Germany’s fast-growing industry.
entries.note: SECONDARY (book read): van Stuyvenberg (1969) ch.7 ‘Germany’, p.290–291.

entries.label: St Lawrence Island starves, 1878–79: the whalers’ walrus slaughter
entries.loc: St Lawrence Island and Bering Strait
entries.hint: Hunting in Bering Strait had been poor after the winter of 1877–78, and the disaster came in 1878–79. A trading schooner arrived in Honolulu with the report that many natives of the Arctic had died ‘as the result of the killing off of the walrus by whalers’; another trader found all the people dead at three settlements on St Lawrence Island, who had died of starvation because they could not get seal, walrus or whale. A whaler wrote that almost everyone said the walrus slaughter was starving the natives, who had eaten their walrus-skin houses and boats. Bockstoce is cautious about the cause: the revenue cutter’s reports stressed alcohol, which may have been exaggerated to win funds, while the traders stressed the lack of food but disagreed on why.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Bockstoce, Whales, Ice, and Men: The History of Whaling in the Western Arctic (1986), PDF pp.141–143. The cause of the famine is disputed there; the whalers’ walrus slaughter is the traders’ and whalers’ own explanation. Compare fats-1000-1500::ec9 for the Thule hunters’ marine-fat economy.
